analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off the California, Oregon, and Washington coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by 13 Democratic and Independent senators, was sent to the Senate Energy Committee and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from ever issuing a lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in federal waters off California, Oregon, or Washington. It was a response to proposals to expand offshore drilling into Pacific waters that have had no active leases for decades. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities in California, Oregon, and Washington, along with the fishing, tourism, and recreation businesses that depend on an unpolluted shoreline, gain protection from the risk of an oil spill and the industrial activity that accompanies offshore drilling.
analysis.who_benefits_short: West Coast coastal communities and ocean-dependent businesses

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to prohibit the Interior Secretary from issuing any lease for oil or gas exploration, development, or production off the coasts of California, Oregon, or Washington.

The prohibition applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of this section or any other law,' so it would override future administration attempts to open the area to drilling through the normal leasing process.
The bill covers the full Pacific Outer Continental Shelf adjacent to all three West Coast states, not a partial or temporary restriction.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose the chance to bid on and develop new leases in Pacific federal waters, and the federal Treasury forgoes any future royalties from production there. Energy consumers bear a marginal cost from reduced domestic supply, though these waters had no active production.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies seeking new leases

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently forecloses domestic oil and gas development off the West Coast, forgoing potential royalties and energy supply regardless of how technology, prices, or national energy needs change in the future.
It is an absolute, permanent ban written into statute rather than a balanced leasing plan, leaving no mechanism to revisit the decision if circumstances change.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For coastal residents and the tourism and fishing economies of three states, permanent protection from drilling and spill risk is a substantial benefit. The cost falls on the oil industry and on potential federal royalties, and it is modest in practice because no active leases exist in these waters and the industry has shown little recent interest there. The main honest objection is that a permanent statutory ban removes flexibility, but the tradeoff favors protection of a uniquely valuable coastline.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on May 2, 2019, joined by 12 cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, including senators from all three West Coast states.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day of introduction.
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept open the possibility of future Pacific leases that the bill would have extinguished, and no new barriers to offshore drilling were created. West Coast communities gained nothing from the bill's failure, though the status quo of no active leases in those waters continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests, by default

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban offshore oil and gas leasing off the West Coast.

for.name: 12 of 100 senators
for.role: Cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, including West Coast senators Harris, Wyden, Merkley, Cantwell, and Murray
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none chaired the committee considering it.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled in the entire Congress.

against.name: Trump administration
against.role: Executive branch pursuing expanded offshore drilling
against.what_they_did: Proposed a five-year outer continental shelf leasing plan that would open new areas, including Pacific waters, to oil and gas drilling, giving the bill its urgency.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or Independents, with no Republican support; the Republican-chaired Energy Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar them from leasing and developing Pacific federal waters off three states, eliminating any future revenue from that area. Blocking drilling protects coastlines and the tourism and fishing economies that depend on them.

industries.industry: West Coast fishing and seafood industries
industries.note: A permanent ban on drilling reduces the risk of oil spills and drilling activity that could damage fisheries and shellfish beds the industry depends on.
Keeping oil platforms and drilling infrastructure out of West Coast waters protects beaches and ocean views that drive the coastal tourism economy.
